items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “a plate boundary where plates move apart and new crust is formed”.
items.answer: Constructive (divergent) boundary
items.markingKey: Constructive (divergent) boundary: a plate boundary where plates move apart and new crust is formed. [1]

items.stem: Explain the formation of an island arc.
items.answer: Where two oceanic plates converge, the older, denser plate is subducted; it melts as it descends into the mantle (helped by water released from the slab); magma rises to form a curved chain of volcanic islands parallel to the trench, e.g. Japan, the Aleutians, the Mariana Islands.
items.markingKey: 1 mark subduction; 1 mark melting; 1 mark volcanoes; 1 mark example [4]

items.stem: Explain the formation of fold mountains at an oceanic-continental boundary.
items.answer: Denser oceanic plate is subducted beneath continental plate; sediments in the geosyncline/accretionary wedge are compressed, folded and uplifted; magma from melting slab forms volcanoes (e.g. Andes).
items.markingKey: 1 mark per stage [3]

items.stem: Which type of plate boundary is found at the East African Rift?

items.markingKey: Constructive: rift valley with volcanoes such as Kilimanjaro. [1]

items.stem: For each location, identify the type of plate boundary and name one landform found there: A Japan (Pacific and Eurasian/Philippine plates); B Mid-Atlantic Ridge (Iceland); C Himalaya (Indian and Eurasian plates).
items.answer: A: destructive (oceanic-oceanic and oceanic-continental); Japan Trench and an island arc. B: constructive; mid-ocean ridge, fissure eruptions and a rift valley (Thingvellir). C: collision (continental-continental); young fold mountains and the Tibetan Plateau.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each boundary, 1 mark each landform [6]

items.stem: With the help of examples, evaluate the claim that destructive plate boundaries produce a greater variety of landforms than constructive plate boundaries.
items.answer: For: Destructive boundaries produce trenches, island arcs (Japan), fold mountains (Andes, Himalaya), composite volcanoes and plateaux. Against: Constructive boundaries produce mid-ocean ridges, transform faults, rift valleys (East Africa), shield volcanoes, fissure eruptions and new oceans (Red Sea). Conclusion: Destructive boundaries have a slightly wider range because they include three types of convergence, but constructive boundaries create the most extensive landform (the ridge system).

items.stem: What is meant by the term “constructive (divergent) boundary”?
options: A plate boundary where plates slide past each other and crust is neither created nor destroyed.
A long, deep, narrow depression in the ocean floor where an oceanic plate is subducted.
A plate boundary where plates move apart and new crust is formed.
A plate boundary where plates move towards each other and one may be subducted.
items.answer: A plate boundary where plates move apart and new crust is formed.
items.markingKey: Constructive (divergent) boundary: a plate boundary where plates move apart and new crust is formed. [1]

items.stem: A student writes: “Ocean trenches are found at constructive plate boundaries.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Trenches mark subduction at destructive boundaries; constructive boundaries have ridges.

items.stem: Explain why there are no volcanoes at continental-continental collision zones.
items.answer: Both plates have similar low density, so neither is subducted far into the mantle; no melting slab means little magma; crust thickens and is uplifted instead.

items.stem: Explain the formation of a mid-ocean ridge.
items.answer: Plates diverge; pressure is released and mantle rock partially melts; basaltic magma rises and erupts, forming new crust; the hot, less dense lithosphere stands high to form a ridge with a central rift.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per point [3]

items.stem: Explain how palaeomagnetism provides evidence for sea-floor spreading.
items.answer: As basalt cools at the ridge, iron minerals align with the magnetic field; the field reverses periodically; stripes of normal and reversed polarity are symmetrical either side of the ridge, showing crust forms at the ridge and moves outwards.
items.markingKey: 1 mark alignment; 1 mark reversals; 1 mark symmetry [3]

items.stem: Explain why oceanic crust is subducted but continental crust is not.
items.answer: Oceanic crust is basaltic and denser (about 3.0 g/cm³) than granitic continental crust (about 2.7 g/cm³), and becomes colder and denser with age.

items.stem: With the help of examples, evaluate the claim that palaeomagnetism provides the strongest evidence for the theory of plate tectonics. In your answer you may refer to magnetic stripes, GPS and fossils.
items.answer: For: Symmetrical magnetic stripes prove sea-floor spreading and allow rates to be calculated; apparent polar wander curves show continents moved. Against: Other evidence: age of sea-floor sediments, distribution of earthquakes and volcanoes along boundaries, Benioff zones, GPS measurements of plate motion today, fossils and rock matching. Conclusion: Palaeomagnetism was decisive historically, but modern GPS gives the most direct proof, and the theory rests on the combined evidence.

items.stem: Explain the processes involved in the rock cycle.
items.answer: Magma cools to form igneous rock; weathering and erosion break rocks down; transport and deposition of sediments; burial, compaction and cementation form sedimentary rock; heat and pressure form metamorphic rock; melting at subduction zones produces new magma.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per process [5]

items.stem: A student measured the mean crystal size (mm) in three igneous rocks from the same magma: Sample A (from a lava flow at the surface): 0.16 mm. Sample B (from a dyke a few metres wide): 0.8 mm. Sample C (from a large batholith several kilometres below the surface): 9 mm. Explain the relationship between depth of formation and crystal size.
items.answer: Deep intrusions are insulated, so magma cools slowly and crystals have time to grow; lava at the surface cools rapidly, forming small crystals.

items.stem: Explain the arguments for and against the view that rock type is more important than climate in influencing the landscape.
items.answer: For: Granite tors and inselbergs, limestone karst, chalk escarpments and clay vales reflect lithology and structure; jointing controls weathering. Against: Climate controls the type and rate of weathering (deep chemical weathering in the humid tropics, frost in periglacial areas) and the processes shaping slopes; the same rock forms different landscapes in different climates. Conclusion: Rock type sets the potential, but climate determines which processes operate and how fast, so both are essential.

items.answer: Magma generated at ridges and subduction zones forms igneous rock; subduction carries rocks to depth where they melt or metamorphose; collision causes regional metamorphism and uplift, exposing rocks to weathering.

options: Rock formed from deposited particles or organic remains that have been compacted and cemented.
The continuous processes by which rocks are formed, broken down and re-formed over geological time.
Rock formed by the cooling and crystallisation of magma or lava.
Rock changed in form by intense heat and/or pressure without melting.
items.answer: Rock formed by the cooling and crystallisation of magma or lava.
items.markingKey: Igneous rock: rock formed by the cooling and crystallisation of magma or lava. [1]

items.stem: Explain why rock type influences landforms.
items.answer: Resistance to weathering and erosion, permeability and structure (joints, bedding) vary: granite forms tors, limestone forms karst, clay forms lowlands and vales.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per point [3]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain the processes involved in the rock cycle. (b) Explain why rock type influences landforms.
items.answer: (a) Magma cools to form igneous rock; weathering and erosion break rocks down; transport and deposition of sediments; burial, compaction and cementation form sedimentary rock; heat and pressure form metamorphic rock; melting at subduction zones produces new magma. (b) Resistance to weathering and erosion, permeability and structure (joints, bedding) vary: granite forms tors, limestone forms karst, clay forms lowlands and vales.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per process [5] (b) 1 mark per point [3]

items.stem: A student measured the mean crystal size (mm) in three igneous rocks from the same magma: Sample A (from a lava flow at the surface): 0.07 mm. Sample B (from a dyke a few metres wide): 0.9 mm. Sample C (from a large batholith several kilometres below the surface): 9.8 mm. Explain the relationship between depth of formation and crystal size.
items.answer: Deep intrusions are insulated, so magma cools slowly and crystals have time to grow; lava at the surface cools rapidly, forming small crystals.

items.stem: “Rock type is more important than climate in influencing the landscape.” How far do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: For: Granite tors and inselbergs, limestone karst, chalk escarpments and clay vales reflect lithology and structure; jointing controls weathering. Against: Climate controls the type and rate of weathering (deep chemical weathering in the humid tropics, frost in periglacial areas) and the processes shaping slopes; the same rock forms different landscapes in different climates. Conclusion: Rock type sets the potential, but climate determines which processes operate and how fast, so both are essential.

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “a plate boundary where plates slide past each other and crust is neither created nor destroyed”.
items.answer: Conservative (transform) boundary
items.markingKey: Conservative (transform) boundary: a plate boundary where plates slide past each other and crust is neither created nor destroyed. [1]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) In a class discussion, a student says: “Iceland is above sea level because a hot spot coincides with the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Explain the formation of fold mountains at an oceanic-continental boundary.
items.answer: (a) Correct. Extra volcanic output from the plume has built up the ridge above sea level. (b) Denser oceanic plate is subducted beneath continental plate; sediments in the geosyncline/accretionary wedge are compressed, folded and uplifted; magma from melting slab forms volcanoes (e.g. Andes).
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2] (b) 1 mark per stage [3]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain the formation of an island arc. (b) In a class discussion, a student says: “Iceland is above sea level because a hot spot coincides with the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Where two oceanic plates converge, the older, denser plate is subducted; it melts as it descends into the mantle (helped by water released from the slab); magma rises to form a curved chain of volcanic islands parallel to the trench, e.g. Japan, the Aleutians, the Mariana Islands. (b) Correct. Extra volcanic output from the plume has built up the ridge above sea level.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark subduction; 1 mark melting; 1 mark volcanoes; 1 mark example [4] (b) 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: GPS measurements show that the Indian Plate into Eurasia is converging at about 8 cm per year. Explain how the rate of plate movement is measured.
items.answer: GPS receivers fixed to the ground measure changes in position over years; also dating sea-floor rocks and magnetic stripes.

items.stem: GPS measurements show that the Cocos Plate beneath Central America is converging at about 9 cm per year. (a) Calculate how far the plates would converge in 10 million years. (b) Explain why earthquakes occur at a range of depths at this boundary. (c) Explain how the rate of plate movement is measured.
items.answer: (a) 900 km (b) Friction as the slab descends causes earthquakes from shallow depths near the trench to over 600 km deep along the Benioff zone. (c) GPS receivers fixed to the ground measure changes in position over years; also dating sea-floor rocks and magnetic stripes.

items.stem: Assess the view that destructive plate boundaries produce a greater variety of landforms than constructive plate boundaries. In your answer you may refer to trenches, island arcs and fold mountains.
items.answer: For: Destructive boundaries produce trenches, island arcs (Japan), fold mountains (Andes, Himalaya), composite volcanoes and plateaux. Against: Constructive boundaries produce mid-ocean ridges, transform faults, rift valleys (East Africa), shield volcanoes, fissure eruptions and new oceans (Red Sea). Conclusion: Destructive boundaries have a slightly wider range because they include three types of convergence, but constructive boundaries create the most extensive landform (the ridge system).

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “symmetrical bands of normal and reversed magnetism in oceanic crust either side of a mid-ocean ridge”.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain how palaeomagnetism provides evidence for sea-floor spreading. (b) Outline the evidence that continents have moved.
items.answer: (a) As basalt cools at the ridge, iron minerals align with the magnetic field; the field reverses periodically; stripes of normal and reversed polarity are symmetrical either side of the ridge, showing crust forms at the ridge and moves outwards. (b) Fit of continents (South America and Africa); matching rock types and mountain belts; fossils (Mesosaurus, Glossopteris); glacial deposits in now-tropical areas; palaeomagnetism.

items.stem: What is meant by the term “sedimentary rock”?
options: The continuous processes by which rocks are formed, broken down and re-formed over geological time.
Rock formed from deposited particles or organic remains that have been compacted and cemented.
The processes of compaction and cementation that turn sediments into rock.
Rock changed in form by intense heat and/or pressure without melting.
items.answer: Rock formed from deposited particles or organic remains that have been compacted and cemented.
items.markingKey: Sedimentary rock: rock formed from deposited particles or organic remains that have been compacted and cemented. [1]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) In a class discussion, a student says: “Limestone and chalk are both sedimentary rocks made mainly of calcium carbonate.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) A revision website states: “Basalt and granite form from the same type of magma.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Correct. They are formed largely from shells and skeletons of marine organisms. (b) Not correct. Basalt forms from basic (low silica) magma; granite from acidic (high silica) magma.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain the processes involved in the rock cycle. (b) Explain how the rock cycle is linked to plate tectonics.
items.answer: (a) Magma cools to form igneous rock; weathering and erosion break rocks down; transport and deposition of sediments; burial, compaction and cementation form sedimentary rock; heat and pressure form metamorphic rock; melting at subduction zones produces new magma. (b) Magma generated at ridges and subduction zones forms igneous rock; subduction carries rocks to depth where they melt or metamorphose; collision causes regional metamorphism and uplift, exposing rocks to weathering.

items.answer: Basic: basalt (A), gabbro (C). Acidic: rhyolite (A), granite (C).
